Theme

School & learning

comparative noun and adjective

degree of an adjective or adverb

also comparative degree, in the comparative, comparatives

classical

Quint. 1.5.45 (Lewis & Short s.v. comparātiō: “the comparative degree”; s.v. superlātiō: per comparātiōnēs et superlātiōnēs)
Traupman 245

comparātiō, comparātiōnis f.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

a comparative form

Quintilian’s word for comparative forms, beside superlātiō for superlatives. In the comparative is comparātīvē or in comparātiōne (Traupman 245).

Other words

  • comparātīvus, comparātīvī m. — the comparative degree

    noun, second declension · also used · late Latin · Don. p. 1745 P. (Lewis & Short s.v. comparātīvus); Traupman 232, 245 · Declension on Wiktionary

    The later grammarians’ gradus comparātīvus, or the adjective alone: doctior (Traupman 232). Quintilian already calls comparative words comparātīva, neuter plural (9.3.19, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • similiter in vocābulīs et nōminibus fit soloecismus genere, numerō, propriē autem cāsibus … huic partī subjungātur licet per comparātiōnēs et superlātiōnēs

    likewise in nouns a mistake is made in gender, number and above all case … to this part one may add mistakes in comparatives and superlativesQuint. 1.5.45

See also degree of comparison, superlative, adjective, compare.

SourcesLewis & Short: comparatio · Lewis & Short: comparativus
